sections.h: Jesus dies as the Passover lambs are killed (John 18–19)
sections.b: In John the priests will not enter the Praetorium so that they can still eat the Passover (John 18:28), and Jesus is condemned at noon on "Preparation Day for the Passover" (John 19:14), the hour when, according to Philo, the Passover sacrifices began in the Temple. A hyssop branch lifts the sour wine to him (John 19:29; Exodus 12:22), and his legs are not broken: "No bone of his will be broken" (John 19:36; Exodus 12:46). Matthew, Mark and Luke instead make the Last Supper a Passover meal, so that Jesus dies on the feast day itself. Scholars disagree over which dating is historical, whether the two can be reconciled, and how much John's timing is shaped by his theme of Jesus as the Lamb of God.

common: John dates the crucifixion to the day before Passover, while the other Gospels make the Last Supper a Passover meal.
uncommon: Annie Jaubert proposed that Jesus followed a priestly solar calendar like that at Qumran, so both dates could be right.

sections.b: John's account is the most restrained in its suffering and the most royal in its meaning. Jesus carries his own cross (John 19:17), is crucified between two others under a sign in Hebrew, Latin and Greek naming him "the King of the Jews" (John 19:19–20), entrusts his mother to the disciple he loved (John 19:26–27), and dies with the words "It is finished" (John 19:30). A soldier's spear brings out blood and water (John 19:34), which John stresses with an eyewitness's oath (John 19:35). The Gospel had already called the cross Jesus' being "lifted up" and glorified (John 3:14; John 12:32–33).

common: The heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan, found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem in 1968, still has a nail through it.

sections.b: John tells of an empty tomb with the grave cloths lying in place (John 20:5–7), of Mary Magdalene meeting Jesus in the garden (John 20:11–18), of Jesus coming through locked doors, showing his hands and side, and breathing the Spirit on the disciples (John 20:19–23), of Thomas's doubt and confession (John 20:24–29), and of a breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:1–14). The risen body can be touched and can eat, yet it is not bound by doors. Jesus' blessing on "Blessed are the ones who did not see, and yet believed" (John 20:29) speaks to every later reader.

John gives Pilate more space than any other Gospel. The trial moves in and out of the Praetorium, with Pilate going back and forth between Jesus inside and the accusers outside. He asks "What is truth?" (John 18:38), three times declares he finds no charge against Jesus (John 18:38; John 19:4; John 19:6), and shows him beaten and crowned: "Look: the man" (John 19:5). Pressed with the threat that freeing him would make him no "Friend of Caesar" (John 19:12), he gives way, but refuses to change his sign. Readers disagree whether John portrays a weak man, a cynical one, or a skilled governor who mocks the Jewish leaders into declaring, "We have no king except Caesar" (John 19:15).

uncommon: Helen Bond reads John's Pilate as strong and manipulative, not weak.

sections.b: In the trial, "the Jews" usually means the chief priests and their guards (compare John 19:6 with John 19:12), not the Jewish people; Jesus, his mother and his disciples are all Jews, and Jesus says salvation comes from the Jews (John 4:22). Yet John's wording, read without this context, was used for centuries to blame all Jews for Jesus' death. The Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council taught that his passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today (Nostra Aetate 4), and most churches now teach the same.

Only John places Jesus' mother at the cross. Jesus says to her, "Woman, look: your son," and to the disciple he loved, "Look: your mother" (John 19:26–27). Many read this as a son's care for a widowed mother. Catholic and Orthodox teaching also sees in it Mary given as mother to all disciples, and some Protestant readers see the beginning of a new family of faith formed at the cross. She is called "woman" here and at Cana (John 2:4), the only two places she appears in John.

sections.h: The Spirit breathed on the disciples (John 20:22)
sections.b: On Easter evening Jesus "breathed on them. 'Receive the Holy Spirit'" (John 20:22), using the verb of Genesis 2:7, where God breathed life into the first human. Readers relate this gift to Pentecost in Acts 2 in different ways: as a first gift followed by a fuller one, as John's version of the same event, or as a sign of what Pentecost would bring.

sections.b: In John the risen Jesus tells his disciples that if they forgive anyone's sins, "those sins have been forgiven them," and if they hold anyone's sins, they are held (John 20:23). Catholic and Orthodox churches see here the institution of the sacrament of confession; Lutheran and Anglican churches keep private confession and absolution; Reformed and Baptist readers see the authority to declare God's forgiveness through preaching the gospel and church discipline.

Peter cuts off the ear of the high priest's slave (John 18:10), then denies Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire (John 18:15–18, 25–27). He runs to the empty tomb (John 20:3–8), plunges into the sea to reach the risen Jesus (John 21:7), and beside another charcoal fire is asked three times, "Do you love me?" Each time Jesus gives him the shepherd's charge (John 21:15–17), then foretells his death and says, "Follow me" (John 21:19). Churches differ over whether this commission gives Peter a primacy that continues in the bishops of Rome.

Jesus called himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). After the resurrection he hands the care of his flock to Peter, while still calling them "my lambs" and "my sheep" (John 21:15–17). Peter's letter later urges elders to shepherd God's flock under the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:2–4).

Jesus tells Peter that when he is old he will stretch out his hands and be taken where he does not want to go, and John explains that this pointed to "the sort of death by which Peter would bring glory to God" (John 21:19). Early Christian writers, including Tertullian and Eusebius, report that Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero.

sections.h: "My kingdom does not come from this world" (John 18:36)
sections.b: Before Pilate, Jesus says his kingdom does not come from this world, or his guards would be fighting for him (John 18:36), and he tells Pilate that his power was "granted to you from above" (John 19:11). Christians have read these words to support nonviolence, the separation of church and state, or the God-given but limited authority of rulers.
